There has been some unsatisfactory refereeing this Reason, and that has no doubt prompted Mr. Edmund Osborne, a member of the Warriegton committee t write"Veteran"of the "Dispatch"on the subject of help- ing the referees by conferring twee duties upon the linesman. Mr. Osborne, letter is as follows

Is it not getting time that the referees were relieved of some of their responsibility, and more power pieced in the hands of the touch judges ? The Northern Union game, as it is being played to-day, is ever an much faster than it used to be, and there are very few referees who are capsble of fo'.owing it cloraly enough to detect all the infringenuentsof the rules.

According to the Inca of the game "The touch judges shall carry flags, and shall each take one side of the ground outside the field of play, son their duty shall be to hold up their Hag when and where the ball goes into touch, or touch-in-goal. . . . It shall be the duty of a touch-judge to report to lb. referee any foul play or obstruction which may have escaped toe notice of tat Now, it is impossible for the referee to notice everything. Time and again forwnrd passes are allowed logo unnoticed, and I would like to siiggert that the touch judges ehould be empowered "to hold up their flag" when forward passes are given within the ten Senile area from the touch line. The referee would then confine himself more closely to the game in mid-field, and would not be expected to do evens." I am certain that the cause Of so much annoyance of spectators would in avoided by adopting some such method, and theirs would be term renson tor complaint. •
hope you will raise a dlscusaion—or, at any rate, give us your opinion wiih regard to the principle.

Mr. Osborne has raised rather a contentious topic. In the main he advocates giving additional powers to the touch-judge, one ef which shall be the holding up of his flag for forward passe, within the ten yards ateal'oesibly such a lute would have saved Warrington a point last Saturdsy, but Ido not think it would opeinte well as a rule. For instsnce. during a passing run down the field, the touch-judge is left a long way behind and is rarely up with the play. Supposing he went into training and sprinted parallel with a centre vad wing who were exchanging pas-es en the inn, he wculd look ridiculous more often than uct.

Then, emppceing further, that he detected a forward nass, or thought be did. In all probability the Referee would have a different .`WWWI on the matter unless he and the players and the touch-judge were dead in line with one snot her—nnalmoat inconceivable possibility. Whose ruling would be law—the touch' judge's or the refer ,'s? This bring us to the crux ef the question. It would never do, in my opinion, to hand over such powers to the touch-judges. The referee west be aide judge. Fun thermore, if the touc'i-judge were merely to raise his flag as a hint to the referee and leave the decision to hint, we should have confusion worse confounded for the players wt,id never know when to stop and when to go on.

What we want is better refereeing, and more thoroughly-trained referees. It is the men tri,ll the whistle who are iinsatisfactory and not the rules. Men like Mr. Newton and Mr. MeCuteheon can referee a game to perfr-tion. The object and it is for the Union to consider—should he to raise the other referees to the same standard. Whet the tench-judges might reasouebly do—sod I agree with

"Veteran " here—would be to draw prompt attention to the frequent obstruction of a kicker when the referee has perforce to follow the flight of the ball. They have such power now, but the referee has the option of acting. If the touch•judge intervenes for obstruction rr rough play then it ahould be binding upon the referee to Pee that the proper penalty in imposed. This is about the only amendment to the rule, as at present existing. which I think would be a real advantage.

div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
(By Redcap )
LAST YEARS RESULTS.

I is purely the utility aspect of the poultry industry that I want to look at for a while. Last year's results shovres a decided progress. Not only was there a greater demand for English products lint also a greater supply. Dealers in foreign products have had to torn their attention more than ever to an it:creasing demand f,r home fell poultry and fresh labl ego-. Now this is a good sign sod much ! marked proaress must have a cause. I could give it ' in a sentence. I will do, Ind then we will analize the cause. Here we are: The progress of the prultry industry to caused by the fact, that knowledge in gradnallv displacing ignorance firm has this knowledge been spread? Wh I have we to thank for a Lever technical understanding in I he arta of potetry farming? Very largely we are indebted to the joint elf rts of the National Poultry Organisation Soeiety and the Agricultural Organisation Society. Con- jointly these two societies hive done a vast SIMI uot Of valuable educational wore during the post year. div.head: MOTOR CYCLES.
div.p: MOTOR CYCLES.

The section of the trade engaged in the manufacture of Motor Cycles affords an interesting and recent example of the recovery of a British trade. In the early part of the last decade the imports of Motor ICycles and parts increased somewhat I rapidly and the exports appear to have decreased. It was only in the year 1907 that the British manufacturers got the upper hand, since which year the imports have gone down appreciably while the exports have gone up, and that rapidly. In 1910 we exported four times as many as in 1907.

THIS WEEK'S STORY.

Throughout his youthful career it has been Willie's lot to wear out all his father's cast-off clothes, cut down and made over. Consequently his appearance was never very suggestive of the height of fashion, but this Willie did not mind, until matters got quite beyond a joke. Then he was found crying bitterly and resentfully in a coal- cellar. When asked what was the matter, he replied: "Father's gone and shaved his face clean, and now, I s'pose I shall have to wear all those red whiskers." POOR LITTLE NOBODY'S CAT. Wretchedly homesick, frightened, forlorn,
She pees through 'the" window' s with 'wistful great eyes ; 0, the quiet within; all in vain does she mourn, Abandoned, downed, unheeded her cries— Poor little nobody's cat!
Once she was petted; soft hands frnoothed the coat So glossy and sleek, now all cobwebs and burrs; What visions of past joys before her eyes float 1 When milk and good meat in abundance were hers—

div.p: LOCAL TRAIN TRAGEDY.
AN APPEAL FOR THE GREENLEES FAMILY
The Mayor Opens a Fund.

Sir, - I am sure tny fellow townsmen and tow es- women will be moved by the sad story which wan told before the Coroner's Court yesterday relative to the death of Eduard Greenlee., as the result of the I mishap at Earlestown Station. Sad as are the circumstances connected with the result of the accident, after tireenle, had fought no bravely against pain and miafortene, the facts ielat- ing to the home he has left 'Jellied are still more moving. Four young people, already without a mother, are now deprived also of their father, and something must be done to provide for their future welfare.

I have been asked, and I gladly secede, to open a hind to provide for the immediate needs of the ease and to put the children in the right way permanently. Friends - including the Citizens Guild of Help have interested themselves in the matter, and I now app.' for subscriptions to aid them in their good work.

ThE FROORKISS OF THE MOVEMENT' Mr. R. Hopwood then gave a racy and inform- ing address on the aims of the loung Liberal movement. and the success which it is achieving throughout the country. He pointed out t.hqt. the League was independent of all other organrsations and pursued Its own policy, taking whatever action it deemed advisable in the interests of Liberalism .and progress. The League existed to train Young Liberals for polities by systematic study of the rroblems of citirenship, and to create a fighting force of active workers for Liberal and progressive principles among young men and women. There were 450 branches of the League in England and Wales, and the membership was something like 200.000. All the branches in Lancashire and Cheshire were joined together in one great Federation, and there were frequent meetings and lectures in the various towns. The branches in Lancaehire and Cheshire numbered over one hundred, with a membership of over twenty thousand. Young Liberalism was based on true demoaracy, and he claimed that it was the chief educational and propaganda organisation of the party. If the Warrington branch marched right at the front and got into the tiring line, holding open-air meetings throughout the spring, summer, and autumn, if they would do their duty, victory wild be theirs, and Mr. Crosfield would be at the top of the poll next time. The first measure of the new Conservative Govern- ment—a Bill to reform the House of Lords and insti- tute the Referendum—was introduced at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society in Cairo-street Church Parlour on Wednesday evening by Alderman'A. Bennett (Secretary of State for the Colonies). There was a large attendance, and the debate yielded many interesting points. Under Alderman Bennett's scheme the House of Lords will include fifty Peers elected by the Peery of the United Kingdom to represent them in the Upper House; NO representatives of the House of Commons 'to be chosen from past and present members of the House of Commons and others who have held high offices of State ; Princes of the Royal Blood ; the Lords of Appeal; the Poet Laureate ; persons who hate at any time acted as Premiers, Governors Ac, of the Colonies, Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, Commander-in-Chief of the Home or Indian Armies, and First Sea Lord; twelve representatives of the various Churches of the United Kingdom ; twenty-five representatives of the leading Universities and learned societies ; one representative of each County Council and County Borough Council; Imperial representatives directly recommended by the Government of India and the various Colonies It iv provided that in the event of any disagreement between the two Houses, they shall meet in ('ouference in the Hall of Westminster or some other convenient place, either as a whole or through selected repre- sentative., and endeavour to arrive at an adjustment of the various matters in dispute between them. Should they ultimately fail to agree, the measure in dispute shall be referred to the people in the final shape in which it left the House of Commons, unless the Government decides to adopt the alternative of resignation. In case of a Referendum each elector shall be entitled to bne vote only, end ntmsll vote by ballot, either " For " or " Against " the measure no referred.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SAITRDAY, JANUARY 213. 1911.

In the official report o JAPAN 'AND the speech of Count TARIFFS. KOMERA, the Foreign Minister of Japan, it is remarked that negotiations are proceeding with the various Powers for the revision of treaties in a direction which will establish a complete tariff autonomy for Japan, and eliminate all unequal engagements. " Notably," Count KONIURA added, "discus- sions with the British Government on the proposed treaty are proceeding favour- ably, and the Imperial Government confidently look forward to the con- clusion at no distant date of a new I treaty satisfactory to both parties alike." , The reference in this last declaration is, of course, not to any tariff treaty; but to the engagements entered into between this coun- try and Japan under the last Government. We are in the happy position of not needing to negotiate tariff treaties. We can use our influence to bring about the lowerinrof tariff walls, but it is not necessary for us to enter into any huckstering on the subject ; nor, in fact, are we able to do so, for we impose no tariff ourselves except for purposes of revenue, and therefore, as we freely offer the fullest advantages to other nations, we have nothing to give away in exchange for special privileges. ' It would be easy to erect a great national grievance on these simple facts. Indeed, that is what is being habitually done by our Protectionists. When Lord LANSDOWNE began to turn a favouring face to the Tariff" Reform" movement he expressed a desire to handle what he called a " big revolver." His mean- ing was that he wished to be in a position when any other country put up tariffs against ourselves to be able to use threats such as might bring about their reduction. In other words, he desired to enter, when occasion offered, into the most foolish and useless of all conflicts, a tariff war. The case was put very bluntly and crudely the other day by another leading member of the Tory Party, Japan has just been revising its tariffs, and it is certainly the fact that it has not treated Ithis country with special consideration on the ground that it is in alliance with us in regard to some other matters, The observa- tion made by the eminent Conservative to whom we have referred was to the effect that if we had tariffs of our own we should be in a position to make a special bargain, to our own advantage, with Japan, which is a neat enough expression of the fallacy which led Lord LANSDOWNE to talk about the "big revolver."

Now, we should he very pleased to meet with any Conservative politician who could tell us what special advantages we should gain if we were now living under a system of Tariff" Reform," and could therefore haggle with Japan as to what the tariffs should be on this and on that. As matters stand, Japan is compelled, in the absence of any tariff treaty whatever, to give to us any advantage that is given to any other country. Our rela- tions on these matters are those of the most- favoured-nation clause. In whatever direc- tion, and under whatsoever compulsion of "big revolvers," Japan lowers its tariff they are at the same moment automatically lowered to ourselves. In vulgar but expres- sive phrase, no other country can get "a pull I over us." That is one side of the question. Here is another. Were we in a position to say to Japan, "We will lower our tariffs on certain artieles of yours if you will lower your tariffs on certain of our own products," and were the response favourable, what

The temporary reverse A LEAD FOR which the progressive LOCAL LIBERALS. forces in Warrington

suffered at the last election has not induced a spirit of dull despair. On the contrary there was never a more encouraging display of enthusiasm and determination in the Liberal ranks than at the present moment, and the work of perfecting the party organisation in readi- ness for the next campaign has already begun. Mr. A. H. Crosfield is giving a characteristically cheerful and vigorous lead and during the past week he has addressed two important political gather- ings. On Saturday, accompanied by Mrs. and Miss Crosfield, the ex-Member attended a smoking concert at the Liberal Club, which, by common consent, was one of the most successful of a long series of social functions associated with this popular centre of Liberalism. A high-class musical pro- gramme occupied the major part of the evening, but Mr. Crosfield took occasion to deliver a terse and inspiring speech, showing -how thoroughly the Liberal Government has warranted the confidence of the democracy by its measures of reform on behalf of the children, the workers, and the aged. War- rington has now a promising branch of the National League of Young Liberals and, judging by tho crowded and enthusiastic gathering at the inaugural meeting on Tuesday evening, there is much to hope from this body of young politicians who will undertake educational and other much-needed work in the constituency. The members were favoured with the presence of Mr. A. H. Crosfield and Mr. J. H. Whitworth (who fought a splendid battle against great odds in the Knutsford division). Their speeches, which sounded an eminently fitting note, were listened to with deep interest. Mr. Crosfield reviewed the political situation in cogent and forceful style and emphasised how successive Board of Trade returns have com- pletely knocked the bottom out of the tariff " reform '• case. He further touched upon the Constitutional issue and the unhappy straits to which the Opposition has been reduced in its futile endeavour to divert attention from the real meaning of the people's verdict—that the veto of the House of Lords must go! Mr. Whitworth gave a fine exposition of Liberal principles which he rightly identified with freedom for the individual to develop his faculties to the best advantage. Young Liberals have some- thing to fight for and we believe they are destined to become a power to be reckoned with in local political life.

Lady Gretnall in the Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform journal on the question of unemployment we did not anticipate that she would join issue with us in a political controversy, but we did think that, for the sake of truth and accuracy, she would have ascertained the facts and admitted herself in the wrong with that generosity which has, of late, been con- spicuous among her political opponents. But Her Ladyship has maintained a silence on the subject which is as profound as that of the sphinx. What she wrote over her own „i signature was the following:— We feel bitterly the disgrace it Sr great f country for such thou l sands of w gmeo to , be nut of employment, when we ha w p this is not the ease in other countries where a tariff is placed on foreign manufactured goods. In common fairness Lady Greenall ought 11 either to substantiate or withdraw such a , sweeping statement. Otherwise she will lay herself open to the charge of having wilfully misled the members of the Women's Tariff Reform League, who doubtless attach some importance to what she has to say on so vital a topic. Mr. Crosfield, very properly and very courteously, took up Lady Greenall's assertion in his speech to th, junior Liberals on Tuesday evening. He drew her attention to the official reports of British consuls in protected countries, particularly Germany, which _

reports reveal a totally different state of things existing in regard to employment there, as compared with her Ladyship's statement. Mr. Crosfield gave some striking quotations,which we supplement with others equally authoritative and convincing. For instance our Consul-General in Berlin, in his report for 1908, says: " The rush on the public Labour Exchanges in Berlin, as well as in the whole German Empire, was almost everywhere greater than in the previous year." The Consul-General for Dusseldorf says : •• The main feature, of the year If were bad pr:ces and, in consequence, want of employ- ment. . . The unumplo)ed queation has become • burning one." If further facts are needed to convince Lady Greenall of the misleading character of her statement,perhaps the following illumin- ating figures will suffice. They record the number of applications in one month, at the German Labour Registries, for every 100 vacant situations as follows: tinid:filed Labourers 348 Machine and Instrument Makers Wood and Carving Industries Traffic Industry 1591 Lea. her Industry Metal Industry / 300 Stone and Earth Industry Building Industry 331 This means that instead of there being

"two jobs for one man" in a leading manu- facturing country "where a tariff is placed on foreign manufactured goods," there were nearly five men looking for every vacant berth. If Lady Greenall requires more evidence to cow, ince her that she is wrong, we shall be happy to supply official informa- tion relating to the serious evil of unnmploy- ment in other countries enjoying the boon (?) of Protection. A little study of the prices of the necessaries of life abroad, as compared with England, might also be of advantage to her Ladyship when next she is called upon to give a lead to the deluded ladies of the Tariff Reform League.

There seems to linger A TORY in the minds of a large DELUSION. Section of' the Tory party the delusion that the present is an opportune moment for settling the constitutional question by com- promise. The "Daily Telegraph,"for example, declares that "the principle upon which the two parties were for so many years divided has practically disappeared," and "the sins to be kept in view may be defined by states- men of either of the regular parties in terms which would be accepted by the vast bulk of I both." The frame of mind which enables the Tori4o to believe that the negotiations which broke down last year can be revived all over agerel is very peculiar.

-W:ien the bL-n-ference on the constitutional question discovered that there was an unbridgeable gulf between the two Parties, an appeal to the country was inevitable. If the Tory party still fail to realise the signi- ficance of that appeal, they must be a "stupid party" indeed. The solution of the consti- tutional question embodied in the Parliament Bill had been before the country for months. Public opinion had been concentrated upon the question almost exclusively, since it was the one feature of the year's politics. The country was not voting merely upon broad general principles. It was not deciding the issue whether the Veto of the House of Lords should or should not be controlled and restrained. That issue was conceded by the Opposition before the election began. What the country had before it was two alternative plans for dealing with the House or Lords question, and the result of the election meant that the electors had chosen he plan put forward by the Government.
We see (says CHURCH SCHOOLS th e " Westminster AND EFFICIENCY. Gazette") that

... Churchmen are com- plaining because some Church schools are finding it difficult to live up to the standard of efficiency required of all elementary , schools. The Bishop of Liverpool yesterday I said " they were told that because these schools, which were built seventy or one hundred years ago, were not up-to-date, they must now be closed." Archdeacon Madden at the same meeting said that " as a result of the policy of ' bloodless administration ' in Liverpool, the schools closed, and those condemned meant that 7,000 Church of Eng- land children would be dispossessed and would have to find places in council schools." Mr. Lathbury in the" Morning Post" takes the same point. "Church schools," he says, "are being taken away": They Cr, being shut up because they do not fulfil the lahr4 requirements of the Loudon County. Council sod the board of Education. These in always something wrong with them...yen if A is only that the aceolamod.tion for the hate aud cops of the pupils is defective. This last sentence makes us feel at least sixteen years younger, for the "hats and caps" were very familiar missiles of attack when Mr. Acland was Education Minister, from 1892 to 1895.

Now these complaints seem to us very ill-conceived. A Unionist predecessor of Mr. Acland, as long as twenty years ago, declared that the time had come when all elementary schools must be judged by one and the same standard of efficiency; since that time, by the Act of 1902, the Church schools have been put on the rates, and all the Church has to do is to provide and maintain the building. Now we are told that it is hard lines, and unfair and unjust to expect that the building should be as good as certainly it would have to be if it were the building of a Council school. For our part we think the Church ought to make it a point of honour not to allow its buildings to be less suitable than those of any other kind of elementary school.

A spc,, r hailing from Liverpool, at the Sunday :•,choul Teachers' Conference held at Warrington, on Monday, made rather an amusing slip. "I have always had to eana my own living," he said, "and so have never been a school teacher." Rather hard on the school teachers present, eh?

Mr. Crosfield was unconsciously respon- sible for an excellent joke at the meeting of Junior Liberals. He said that he would like to continue to be a Junior Liberal, " but Anno Dmnini would tell." Several members who are acquainted with a certain lady's name, smiled a smile which must have puzzled the speaker._ _

' Warrington has enjoyed a few brief hours of sunshine during the past week, and inspired by the cheering rays, it occurred to us that there would be opportunity to test the accuracy of the new sun dial in Queens 'Gardens to commemorate the visit of King Edward. The pillar has been a familiar object fur a long time past, and the discovery that there is no dial plate came as a shock. Can it be that the grave and reverend seignors who manage our affairs have for- gotten all about it?

Owing to the defeat of Mr. Oswald Partington. who was prevented by ill-health from taking any part in the contest in his constituency, Mr. William Jones has been appointed a Junior Whip. Mr. Jones had previously acted as Parliamentary private secretary to the Government Chief Whip, and by his indefatigable energy has rendered admirable service to the Party. His inter- ventions in debate have not been very frequent, and will be rarer still now, but the House of Commons has always heard with pleasure a speaker who possesses a gift of real eloquence.

Mr. Holman Kingdon makes a suggestion in our correspondence columns, which will, at any rate, have the warm approval of local tradesmen. "If a London all-British Shopping Week," he says, '' Why not a Warrington one?" Echo answers, why not? We understand that shop-keeping in Warrington nowadays is by no means a sure and easy road to fortune. Perhaps some of our readers—tradesmen and others —will favour us with their views on the new idea.

The following pathetic incident is unfor- tunately quite true. The "Manchester Guardian" vouches for it. A young bank manager and his wife, who live over one of the Manchester branches of a well-known bank, had a beautiful cat. He was a great favourite, and when he died the other day it was agreed that the body must be given a decent burial. Accordingly the husband decided to take it out into the country to a pleasant spot where they often took their walks, and there to inter it. He put the body in a large silver-bag, which had, as is usual, the name of the bank printed on the outside, and took the tram for the intended spot. When he reached his stopping-place he got up and turned to pick up the bag. It was gone. The man who "let the cat out of the bag "would not be gratified.

The Hon. Harry Lawson, M.P., against whose return for Mile End by a majority of two votes a recount and scrutiny have been granted to the petitioner, has had a very remarkable electioneering record. At a by-election for the Cirencester Division of Gloucestershire, in October 1892, Mr. Lawson stood as a candidate in the Radical interest against Colonel Chesters Master who was declared elected by three votes. On a scrutiny it appeared that the candidates had an equality of votes, but that the returning officer could not give a casting-vote, as his functions were at an end on the declaration of the poll. The election was a nullity, and on the issue of a writ for a fresh election Mr. Lawson was returned. Mr. Lawson who as a Radical was a petitioner in a recount when defeated by three votes, is now, as a Conser- vative. a respondent in a recount when returned by two votes. This must surely constitute a record in the vicissitudes of electioneering and party contests.

We offer our hearty congratulation to )Jr. and Mrs. Bainforth on the high attainments of their sen,and we shall look foraard with pleasure to further succe,s. Local wedding The marriage was solemoized on Thursday after- noon at the Be wsey-road Wesleyan C hurch of Miss Alice Dickinson,daughter of Councillor Dickirtecon,of Ramsey. street and Mr. Charles Frederick Wood, of Wildsrs- I Causeway. The Rev. E. B. Keying officiated. F. bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr. Alban Dickinson. was attired in a light tweed costume and velvet toque. The bridesmaids were 'Misses E.Dickinson and Heath. The 'former wore a Ilight tweed costume with black picture hat, and the latter wore a dark tweed costume, with a hat of a similar kind. Mr. J. B. Wood (brother of the bride- groom) discharged the duties of best man. Tbe reception was hell at the home of the bride's parents, after which the happy couple left for Southport, where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling attire was a blue serge costume. Numerous presents were received, including one from Mr. Wood's colleagues at the Inland Revenue Office, Manchester. Woos Fire at Wilder:pool. On Sunday morning shortly after six o'clock, a fire broke out in a shed balonging to Messrs. Oreenall Whitley and Co. in Greenali'savenue and in which there earn 40 to 50 woad pressed straw. A signal- ' man named Fred Sumners, residing in Old Loodon-1 n ad, first noticed the out-break and gave the alarm by the ringing of the fire bell. Mr. Albert Broady, the manager of the stables, who lives close at band, was 80012 on the spot and, fortunately. IS valuablel horses in the adjoining stable. were at once got not ' , and placed in a position of safety. The firemen, who arrived under the direction of the deputy-supsrin- tendent, Mr. Craughton, arrived, but it was found impossible to save the straw which was completely ruined by fire and water, the I,es being estimated by Mr. Broady at from £l5O to ,C2OO. 'I he speaker pointed out that the Americans coined the title, and claimed Emerson as the High Priest of their new cult, but he (the speaker) explained that " The New Thought " was even older than the times of Emerson. It was found in the Old and New Testaments As a man thinketh so is he "and " Out of the heart man spealteth." Adult School, Bewsey. On Saturday evening last an interesting limelight lecture was given by Mr. Dunlop, curator of the Warrington Museum, on Spiders." Commencing with the egg stage, the lecturer proceeded through the various stages of spider life and habits, and gave a wonderful account of the ingenious way the spiders proceed in the making of the webs.---Mr. Dunlop is to visit the school again in February, when be will give a lecture on a natural history subject.—k hearty vole of thanks, passed with acclamation, concluded a most enjoyable evening.—On Sunday morning, Mr. W. Webster, President of the Warrington Field Club, , gave an excellent lecture on " Insect architecture." ' He told those present in everyday language about the wonderful work performed by ants, warps, bees and other insects.—Judging from the intelligent questions asked by members f the class, it showed that a keen interest had been taken in the lecture, and another visit from Mr. Webster will be eagerly looked forward

--- -- Rev. 11. Dunsleo Criticises the Lord MayoP. Speaking on Sunday niuht in Kensington Baptist Chapel, Jubilee-drive, Liverpool, on the " Peace Crusade," the Rev. Herbert Dunnico (formerly pastor of Golborne-street, Baptist Church, Warrington), said that during the past week the Lord Mayor had pre- sided over a meeting of the National Service League, and had commended its objects to the citizens of Liverpool. Ile (the speaker) desired to make an emphatic protest against what was in his opinion a gross abuse of a distinguished and honourable position. The objnet of the National Service League was to introduce into this eountry a form of conscription that Wan hateful to on overwhelming proportion of the British people. It was an unwriiten law, and so far as he knew had never heen violated, that the chief citizen of their city should not give the sanctionof his official position to questions upon which there were such acme differences of opinion. Apart altogether from the question of militarism and anti- militarism, he believed the Lord Mayor had committed a grave error, and had detracted from rather than enhance I the dignity of his office.

div.head: Warrington Women's Liberal Association:
div.p: Warrington Women's Liberal Association:

" Are our Sunday schools efficient?" was be subject under discussion at a meeting of the Warrington Sunday School Teacher's , association on Monday. The question has woused much anxious thought in religious ircles of late. For instance, the Bishop of London has been recommending his clergy to pay greater attention to their Sunday bchools. He has been led to do so by the growing laxity of Sabbath observance, the general indifference to religious education, and no doubt also by the necessity of forming another barrier in the scheme of Church defence. The London "Times," discussing the Bishop's address, suggests that the first step must be in the direction of system and organisation, including regular inspection of methods and results, some kind of guidance, if not actual training, for teachers, with such encouragement to the attainment of proficiency as can be given by a system of inspection or examination with recognition of merit. " Churchpeople, too, must, be prepared to spend money on their Sunday schools. Besides the expenses incident to the improvement of plant, the preparation and printing of syllabuses and other necessary literature, there must be found adequate stipends for qualified inspectors or instructors, and possibly for a nucleus of fully-trained professional teachers. The zeal and devotion of amateurs, upon which the Church has hitherto relied for her Sunday schools, is no longer sufficient in itself. The whole system needs reorganising on something more of a business footing in every diocese—not, we should hope, to the exclusion or discouragement of amateur zeal, ut to its help and support, that it may bring forth better fruit."

div.head: WARRINGTON SOCIETY
div.p: WARRINGTON SOCIETY
Literary Paper by Mr. H Stuart Page.
THE MATERIALISM OF THE AGE.

At a meeting of members of the Warrington Society held in the Old Academy on Monday evening Mr. H. Stuart Page reed a critical may on the Itubsiyat of Omar Khayyam. Mr. E. J. Hall presided over a good attendance. .

Ifr. H. Stuart Page referred to the story of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam as one of the romances of literature. It was written in the original Persian, 800 year. ago, but was unknown to Engiiih literature 80 years ago. "To-day it is one of OA most popular works in the language, he said. 'lts worship has became a cult and its appreciation a fashion." The verses hail not only taken a very firm hold on the leaders of thought and literature, but on the imagina- tion of the ordinary reader as well. The homage paid to the poetry and philosophy of the Ituitairat had reached its culmination in the existence of the Omar Khayyam Club, ti which institutiou belong men of light and leading in every department of thought. Thoee men were devoted to doctrines entirely different from those on which the English character was built. It gave rise to grave misgiving itt the minds of some people to see the irreconcilable p-ssimitm of Omar taking the [dace of the invincible optimism that per- vaded the great body of English poetry. They looked upon the growing appecintion of the Rubeiyat as a sign of national decadence. That was, however, • matter upon which opinion. differed. The conditions under which the Itobaiyst were written were peculiar. The Persian Empire was tottering to its fall ; it. ancient faith was breaking up before the advance of the hordes of 3.lahorriet It was the tine, of the first Cmside and the Cross was contending against the Cresent. .

Mr. Page then traced the career of Omar Khayyam and pointed out that from his death in 1123 until 1853 nothing M. known of his writing. in the , Western world. lit 1853 Profersor Cowed, of Cam- bridge was looking over a bundle of ancient Mallt, scripts in the Bolivian library, when he discovered a beautifully written Persian poem. The profeesor recommended it to his friend Edward Fitzgerald, who had begun to study Persian. Fizgerald had a copy of it made and for several years it was his constant companion. Then he translated the work. Those a position to know have said that be was wonderfully euccessful in reproducing in English the thoughts and phrases of the original as well as in catching the rhythm. The poste was accepted by the editor of an English magazine, but as several months passed and the verses did not appear, Fitzaerald withdrew it. It is believed he could not find a publisher bold enough to publish the poem, because of is audacite of though., to Fitzgerald determined to publish it himself, lie had it privately printed in p.mphlet form end issued it 'n brown paper corers at the price of five shillings. A friendly publisher included it in a catalogue of Oriental works, but this brought -no result. Fitzgerald presented a bookseller with the whole of the copies and though the price was reduced to one shilling, there were no pin-chasers. In deapair the bookseller placed them outside the shop and marked them " All this lot one penny each." lri this manner the poem was brought to the notice of the public. At the present time one of those first copies, when sold by auction, will realize £5O or £6O. Mr. Page then took his audience through the poem almost stanza by stanza, giving • critical explanation aahe proceeded, and dwelling at considerable length on some of the more important pasnages. -11 e , also contrasted the morbid materialistic spirit which pervaded the Rubsiyat with the heroic defiance and indomitable hope which found I express; on in the works of our own poet.. ,In conclusion he said :—And now let us ask pur- -1 selves a very serious question, which is suggested by the present popularity of the Rubaiyat of Omar I Khayyam. Has our national character changed, and are we drifting into acquiescence with the spirit of materialism that pervade. this work? lam afraid we can only answer in the affirmative. One cannot 'study contemporary life without 'seeing evidences of it on every band. Long-cherished ideas and firmly-held convictions have gone by the board ; there hss been a ehipwreck of ideals and those involved have clutched at the 1 materialistic philosophy of Omar as drowning men clutch at a straw. It is an age of growing Incurious- ness and the Eastern symbolism and vuluptuons ribraseolegy of the Rubaiyat soothes it and minitters Ito its sensuousness. It is also an age of devil-may- care materialism which shirks the greatest of all questions by adopting the " a good fellow and 'twill all be well ' attitucle. It is an see that has cultivated an easy-going philosophy of life and the faith of Omar fits it too nicety—hence Iris popularity. (Applause.) An interesting discussion followed and Mr. Page was thanked for his raper cu the proposition of Alderman Bennett seconded by lie. Hallaway.

div.head: VISIT TO WARRINGTON
div.p: VISIT TO WARRINGTON
A Champion of the Shop

In the death of Sir Charles occurred at his London resident day at the age of 68, there pat notable personality who was, at the very forefront of English whom many regarded, in his earl destined to occupy, under the Sovi highest position in the State. c'• possessed one of the most e minds that has ever been dein serious study of politics. He authority and with a remarkable the facts on a great range of subje leg from Labour questions to tl and from foreign politics to the army and navy defence. But with all his power and kno, career was broken in its prime by h tion with a famous divorce sui -.lu air Charles spent the remainder of his days as a private member of Parliament,treated with deference, but beyond the charmed circle of officialdom. Sir Charles visited Warrington nearly ten years ago and addressed a conference of trade unionists • on questions affecting the shopiassistants, of whom he was a great champion in Parliament. A REMARKABLE CAREER. In a brilliant sketch of Sir Charles's career —" a career, strange, momentous, and chequered—full of contrasts of power and of impotence, of hope and of despair "—the " Daily Telegraph" gives some vivid and interesting particulars.

M.P AT 24. Throughout the greater part of his life he had a great love of travel, and it is charac- teristic of that desire for political employ- ment that he should have stood for a Parliamentary seat at a moment when most young men are absorbed in their sports or their amusements; he was only twenty-four when he became a member of the House of Commons. In 1872 he married Katherine Shield,the daughter of a captain in the Army. Miss Sheil—as the name implies—was of Irish blood; she was very beautiful and very attractive, and Dilke gave to her—this hard cold, ambitious, absorbed man—a love that had all the romaaw and fervour of a great passion. In 1874 she bore to him his first and only child—the one who to-day bears his name and his title; but in giving birth to this new young life lost her own. Those who knew Dilke intimately at the time spoke almost with a shudder of the tragic and broken grief of the man. QUEEN VICTORIA'S COMMENT. The days of his youth had a brief period of unrestraint. By some curious freak of self-forgetfulness he developed Republican tendencies and queried the Civil list of the Queen. Commenting on the episode Her Majesty recalled that she had stroked Dilke's hair when he was but a child. "Perhaps," • she said, " I rubbed it the wrong way." THE DIVORCE SUIT.

div.head: WARRINGTON PARISH CHI'RCH CLERGY.
div.p: WARRINGTON PARISH CHI'RCH CLERGY.

The ancient mother Church of Sr. Elnhin, Warring- ton. occripiee a warm place in the affections of the Churchpeopie of Warrington and district, and an excellent work is being carried on there by a devoted gaff of clergy, of whom we present rt photograph above. The Rector (the Rev. Canon F. W. Willis, M.A.) has I'ad charge of the parish since May. IRB.', having been selected for the living by Lord LiHord, the patron. Canon Willis is 3 convinced and sraunch adherent of the Catholic or High Church school, and never hesitates to give utterance to his belief., even at the risk of provoking controversy. His teaching has always been on definite Sacramentarian line.. The aerviceis at the Parish Church are charac,erised lip dignified ceremoniat, without extremes, and there is a choral celebration of the Holy Communion on the first Sunday of every month and on great festival.. Canon Willis, who graduated at Corpus Chrieti College, Oxfold,was ordained deacon in 1817 by the Bishop of Chester and priest in 18,13 by the Bishop of Oxford. After holding curacies at Alderley, 1 Cheshire, Wendover, Bucks, and Rainhill,Lancashire, he became Vicar of All Saints, Wellingborough, in 1572. fle remained there until hie appointuient to St. Elphin's, Warrington, and gained the love and respect of his parishioners to his diligent pastoral work and his elicrts on behalf of Church schools. Speaking of Mr. Willis', departure from the town, a Wellingborough correapondent wrote : " While the promotion of our most popular Vicar is regarded with great satisfaction by bin devoted flock, and by the general public here, his removal will be considered as • distinct loss to the religious, educational and social life of the place." Canon Willis's work in Warrington has been characterised by steady progress in the Church life of the parish and he has endeared himself not only to his own congregation hut to the members of other lennuti-
'Tong,

rmions who, however much they may differ from him slwaya recognise his ,incerity. The day and Sunday schools and various parochial organizations are in a healthy state and there are large congregations at the church services In ISIIS the Rector was appointed to an honorary canonry of Li -erpool Cathedral ; in 1901 he became chaplain to the flishop of Liverpool, and in 1910 he succeeded the Rev. An important addition was made to the objects and ; rules of the L, corp rot Diocesan Cuurch Aid 0 ,ciety at the annual meeting held in the Caurch House, Liver- pool on Nlonday afternoon, with the Bishop of Liver- pool in the chair. The effect of the addition is to enable 1 the society to aid the Church in future by helping to meintain church halls in very puor neighbourhoods. The I Biahop said them were still twenty-four parishes at ; least in the diocese imam the population exceeded 10,000, and where only one curate was at work. This. was heartbreaking. In such conditions the Church of England could not do her work, and it was no wonder that, in come C.., the Nonconformists came in and did the work for her. If the Church of England wee to do her duty in these places& further annual income of £1.200 would be needed to supply extra curates. The Church Peatoral Aid Society gave a block great oil £6,100 for this work, and the Additional Curates' Society gave at least £1,200; but the funds of these two POCielies were stationary. and not many Sew grants could be expected from them. The need must be met by the Church in the diocese of Liverpool, and he could not believe that the diocese which had raised nearly £350,010 towards the building of a cathedral would be content to contribute the very small sum of £1;210 a year towards the necessary and far-reaching work which that society was trying to do in the large and popukeis parishes. div.head: VARIOUS WAYS.
div.p: VARIOUS WAYS.

The mould (which should be from tin. to /in. thick) may be pulled off the foot am soon as the planter begins to get warm in the process of setting. or even m..oner if care is taken. One advantage of pulling off the mould as soon as possible, and before the plaster has become hard, is that any hairs which may not have been proiw rly oiled down are not stuck to the plaster, and con- sequently the paint ul operation of pulllng out the hairs, as in a hard-set mould, is avoided._

Instead of setting the foot on a pillow we cloths, soft clay or modelling wax (procur- able from any artists' colourman) may le need. This will take an impression of the tinder side of the foot, and virtually act as a mould, the mould being then in two pieces, the plaster top and the wax under side. These two pieces may then be tied together. and the east taken in the usual way. Another way is merely to rover with plaster. to a thickness of about lin., the part to ha cast, aa described above, and when set break it off in two or three pieces, which may be joined together al terwards. another way is to immerse the oiled foot in the basin of gauged plaster, and when all is covered. take out the foot and lay on the remaining plaster. The toot may lie released by lay- ing a waxed thread, before the plaster in ate plied. along the top and underneath to the heel, or right round the sides. The waxed thread will stick to the foot, and when the foot has been, plunged in the plaster, and the plaster is nearly set, take up the ends of the thread and rip up the mould, thus divid- ing it into two or four pieces as the can demands. _ _ _
• • • CAST OF A HAND.

To take the mould of a hand is an easy matter. Frequently all that is desired is one side of the hand only, as it may appear when lying on a cushion, and this can be moulded in a single piece. Oil is rubbed over it, especially round and under the nails, and it is laid on a pillow, which may be covered with soft paper. The swellings of the pillow can be so arranged Ant to 611 up most of those under parts which the mould would not "leave." A towel rolled round the arm will limit the mould in that direction. After the plaster has net, the hand, with the mould on it, can be lifted bodily from the pillow, and any edges or tongues of plaster which hinder the pulling out of the hand pared away. When the east of the hand is wanted in the "round "—that is, when both sides are to be completely shown—it can be laid on sand; more an can be packed round it until only so much is left exposed as will allow a mould from it to leave in a single piece. The exposed half is then moulded. the hand and moukt are turned over bodily, and the edges of the mould are trimmed, keylicled, and clay- watered, after the usual manner of walde- moulding in two pieces. The second hall ist Lea moulded.

div.head: TRAIN DISASTER IN WALES.
div.p: TRAIN DISASTER IN WALES.

The terrible railway disaster on the Taff Vale talway in South Wales. Not since October, 1904, when an express was wrecked near Llanelly, with a casualty list of 1 killed and 50 injured, has a Welsh railway been the scene of a catastrophe comparable to that which occurred this week, near Pontypridd, when eleven were killed and 20 Injured. The accident recalls in its general circumstances the recent disasters at Ormskirk and Aisgill. A passenger train crashed into a standing goods train, several coaches were telescoped, Finning the unhappy victims under the wreckage. Among the dead were 3 miners' leaders who were en route to London to attend the national miners' tonlcience.

The Right Rev. Edward Talbot. D.D., the newly appointed Bishop of Winchester. Dr. Talbot is the second son of the Hon. 3. C. Talbot, fourth son of Earl Talbot. He was educated at Charterhouse and Oxford, Where he had a distinguished career. Dr. Talbot is the author of several theological works, a scholarly and earnest preacher, and an incessant worker. He was appointed Bishop of Rochester in 1895, bat on the partition of the diocese in 1905 assumed the title of Bishop of Southwark.

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, MP.
SHOULD OLD AGE PENSIONS BE GIVEN AT SIXTY?

The abolition of the Poor Law disqualifica- tion has been followed by a decline in the number of persons receiving outdoor relief, A good deal of surprise has been expressed at the small number of old folks who have left the workhouses in order to take up and live upon the pension outside. But those who had made a study of this question expected nothing else. In all the scientific calculations which have been made as to the cost of a system of Old Age Pensions it was assumed that only a small number of the af ed inmates of the Poorhouses would come upon the pension list. The reason for that ii obvious to those who will think carefully. The old folks in the workhouses are mainly people without relatives, or without relatives who would care to give them a home, or they are people who,through weakness and illness, are not able to look after themselves. Even bearing in mind how much our Poor houses need to be humanised before they are ideal homes of rest for the aged, it cannot be denied, that apart from sentiment, a great many of the old folks now inside are far more comfortable, are far better fed, and receive better attention than they would be able to get outside. Taking all these things into consideration it is not surprising that few of the workhouse inmates have exchanged their abode for an outside pension.

div.head: REMAINING INJUSTICE.
div.p: A REMAINING INJUSTICE.

With the aged who were getting out-door relief it is different; and when the completed returns for January are issued we sha.il find there is a very large reduction in the n amber of outdoor paupers. The aged person previ- ously receiving poor relief has nothing to lose and everything to gain by claiming a pension. It will only be a matter of a few weeks until outdoor relief to persons over 70 practically disappears. There is one respect, however, in which the poor law disqualification will continue to operate. I called the attention of the Chancellor of the Exchequer to the point by a question in the House of Commons some months ago, and I regret to learn that the fear I then expressed has been justified. A person can- not at the same time receive both poor relief and a pension, and the law has laid it down that poor relief given to a wife is relief given to the husband. There are eases where the wife is under 70, the husband over 70, and up to the end of last year both were in receipt of relief from the Poor Law. If the husband claims his old age pension now the wife must give up getting relief; if she continues to do so the husband is dis- qualified from receiving the pension. The net result is that such a couple are no better off, possibly worse if the relief be entirely foregone. The Chancellor expressed his sympathy with my protest against the injustice of this state of the law and promised to give the point attention when the amendment of the Act is considered. Meanwhile the injustice remains a blot upon the pensions system.

div.head: SOMETHING LIKE A PENSION.
div.p: SOMETHING LIKE A PENSION.

A resolution is to be moved at the Labour Party Conference next week demanding the reduction of the pension age to 60, and the increase of the amount of the pension to 10s. a week for everybody. Such a resolution was passed last year, but this is one of the many instructions given by the Labour Conference to the Labour Party which have not been carried out. Those who are respon- sible for such a resolution can never have thought for a moment what is really meant by the demand they are putting forward. If it is meant, as it seems to be, as a practical ' proposal for immediate adoption than it is ludicrous in its absurdity. There are about four million persons in the United Kingdom over 60 years of age, and to give pensions to all these at the rate of 10s. a week would cost over £100,000,000 a year. If we had a Socialist Government in power, and if the annual income from rent, interest, and profit had been transferred to tbe community, then such a proposal might be reasonably put forward; but to calmly ask for an amend- ment to the Old Age Pensions Act which will add over £100,000,000 a year to taxation is just about the wildest proposal which was ever seriously advanced.

It is easy to make out a strong case for the reduction of the age to 65, and this is an amendment which ought to be pressed as soon as the Infirmity and Unemployed Insurance schemes have been passed. To do this would not cost an impossible sum—at the most probably not more than ten millions, and against this could be set the saving in outdoor relief. The age is 65 in New Zealand and in Australia, and the trade unions in this country which have super- annuation schemes usually fix sixty as the age at which the pension can be claimed. The following table shows, in regard to four of the principal trade unions, the age at which the pension can be claimed, the average age at which the members do claim the pension, the average ago at which the superannuated members die, and the aver- age age at death of the membership as a whole:—

Age at Age St Death of ()oath of Age Est super- 4[4. noral Pengoioe hope, annualed Ago aunustion Member., oh* Bricklayers ... 55 631 68 49 London Compositors 60 631 68 491 Steam engine society 55 63 72 511 A. Society Engineers 60 63 70 541 A man who falls out of work in any one of these trades at sixty years of age stands a very poor chance of ever again getting employment at his job. He is unfit for any other kind of work. The same applies to every class of workmen. The Unemployment Insurance will provide them with a small income until they reach the pension age, but when a man is really past work he ought to be transferred from that fund to the pension fund. I believe it is the intention of the present Chancellor not to have the pension age reduced at all. He thinks the better plan will be to keep it at 70 and to make provision for the needy by the other two schemes—the Infirmity and Unemployment Insurances. But it will be a condition of receiving maintenance from the latter that the person must take employ- ment if it is offered, and that would be a hardship to many I a man who is really past work but has not reached the age of 70. HOW OLD AGE COMES.

After the age of 65 pauperism increases very rapidly. It was shown in a Return furnished a few years ago at the request of Mr. Burt that while the percentage of paupers among the population between the ages of 60 and 65 was ten per cent, of the whole, the percentage between 65 and 70 was twenty per cent. It was stated by the Commission on the Aged Poor that 35 per cent. of the population of London over 65

Besides its registers the Parish Church has some interesting records preserved in its Terrier books and vestry records. It may save our readers a search in the dictionary if we explain that a Terrier book originally described the record made of the services and rents which vassals owed to their lord. In modern use it describes a book in which a list of lands or properties is described. As the Church held glebe lands it kept its own Terrier book. There is a glimmer of interest in sorne prices quoted in connection with the glebe lands. A penny for a hive of bees. it at present pay'il for palatines per acre, and so proportionately for a greater or lesser quantity.

div.p: OUR SERIAL. STORY.
(ALL ILIGHTB RNSIMD.] THE MYSTERY OF ROGER BULLOCK,
TOM GALLON author of " Tattetley," " Meg the Lady."
CuArms XI.
" THU woRLn VORGIMING."

For what seeined a long time Jobe. Roach stared at Richard Bullock —holding the lantern up against hio fare, and evidently striving to get this jew idea firmly in hi. mind. In a stupid fashion he looked at the gravest his feet, and then at the man standing before him ; then he shook Into head in a bewildered way. Richard Bullock," he muttered at last. In the name of all that's wonderful and unholy—where did you come from "I've been coming to you, Mr. Jab. Roach, for quite it long lime," answered the " Like several other people, you've made a slight mistake over the question of a name. It's a long story, and I won't trouble you with it now : suffice it that there were two brothers—Roger and Rich. ord. Richard stands; before yen ; I believe Roger is deed." At this Lasares Ilea began to whimper again, adding sonic half intelligible words to the efitct that he knew nothing whatever about it, and that ho called everyone to wit- ness he had been dragged into the business in.k.t, unwillingly. Richard Bullock glanced quickly from one man to the other—looked at the spades and the pick that lay at feet. Then, as neither of the men replied, he pointed sternly to Iles, and asked— " What is it, llos ?"

"'I he found Roger Bullock under the house here," said Iles, in a shaking whisper —" crrried there by an underground river that flows under the town. The man Neal Jarrow wan there—and Jarrow was afraid— Roger Bullock. lies at your feet." . . . . . .

Rickard Bullock iitot;d with bent head for 3 moment or two, looking at the ground : then he shrugged his shoulders, and sighed heavily. " Wkat an ending !" he said. " And yet I suppose this is for the hint—it the boy's to be saved," he muttered to him. self. Mr. Roach—the air here seems to stifle me ; let us get away from the place. I didn't coin, to speak of this," he went on —"I didn't know that you were concerned in this affair at all. Jarrow is the man I am anxious to meet."

" arrow is the man solely responrible," said Roach, who had by this time recovered himself a little. "'think of my position, Mr. Bullock ; what was I to do, with the body of this man actually snider my house?"
"We won't speak of A. please, said the other quickly. " Now perhaps you will lead the way to the house ; there are accordl matter.; about which I have to talk to you.' , ..

Mr. Roach went on in front, with the lan- tern bobbing at his side ; Iles brought up the rear wilts Richard Bullock. When there was a slight distance between themselves and Roach, Lazarus Iles turned quickly to the man beside him, and whispered. •' Don't trust him ; don't believe any promise he may make." They got to the house, and Jabes Roach went in, the others following. AS they otood together in the little ball, Roach suddenly card that Iles would show the way ; raised the lantern to his face, and puffed out the light. There was . a slight movement in the darkness, and the sudden scratching of a match ; then Richard Bullock looked calmly d•iwn the length of the cigar he was light- he, to see the cild man with his arm up- r iised, and in his hand a heavy oak stick he led caught up from a corner. " You don t object to my smoking, I Lope ?" asked Richard Bullock, looking the disconcerted Roach straight in the eyes. " And I think if I were you I'd put that eack down.'' Roach tossed the stick from him, and followed Iles into the dining-room. It was Richard Bullock who shut the door ; It, was Richard Bullock who, in the calmest fashion poseible, produced a revolver from his breast pocket, and looked at it thought- fully for a moment or two, and then put it

" Ye; will notice, Mr. Roach, that I come Armed," he said. "1 know you to be a peaceable citizen, and therefore that is a liberty I must ask you to excuse. Much bet- ter to have explanations first," he went on, puffing at his cigar. " Now to business. I wrote von a letter some time ago---" " And you signed it 'R. Bullock,'" broke. in the old man. "I've been cheating myself with the belief that you were dead—because Roger Bullock was dead. Of course I'm glad. Mr. Richard Bullock," he added form- ally—" very glad indeed to make your ac- quaintance; I've been quite looking forward tosyour coming ; we've all been looking for- ward to Tour coining—haven't we, Iles ?" "I don t think we need trouble Mr. Ilea to answer," said Richard Bullock. "Per- lisps it will clear the ground a little if I tell you that during the past few days, while you have imagined me dead, I have been able to make enquiries concerning you ; I bare also had the satisfaction of meeting my ward (for Madeline is under my care for the future); and I have discovered quite a num- ber of things about you, Mr. Roach." " Charmed to hear it," snapped the old man. " Perhaps you'd like to know my opi tt itt n of a man who thrusts his nose in when, he's not wanted, and interferes with the business of other people ?" " Your opinion on that matter would not interest me Mr. Roach," said Richard Bul- lock calmly. "What will interest me, in the first place, is to receive from you a full account of Madeline's fortune. I dare say you will remember that she was away from thin house for one whole night recently ?" he added. "I remember it Well," said Roach. " he refused to tell me where she was."

" She was with me," replied the other quietly. "I have Seen staying at the Fisherman's Arms, and s it was nem:nary that Madeline should tell me a lot iihout her- self and about your treatment of her during the 'past ten or twelve years, I arranged with the landlady of that inn' to take charge of her, and to find her a room because, you see, Madeliae nnd I talked very late, and indeed at one time I had thought that I would take her right away from your house, then and there. '

. ..... " Extremely kind of you," muttered Roach sulkily. " However—the more she told me, the more I began to understand that you were a moo to be watched ; therefore I cautioned her to say nothing until I gave her leave to speak. After our pleasant little explana- tan, Mr. Roach,' he went on, smiling upon the other man—" I think I'll see the young lady now, and take her away with me ; this is scarcely the place for her to remain in any longer." Roach suddenly. burst out laughing: "You're a day titter the fair, my friend, he said insolently. " Your precious ward, us you call her, hotted this very night with a man we were detaining here—the man who killed your brother Roger. You can search the house if you like ; there's no one here but ourselves. " What man has she bolted with %" ask- ed Richard Bulloek in amazement, looking from one to the other.
It was Iles who answered the question. "Ills name is Mark Conuaway," he said— you know the man."

„-- -...... Jabez Roach turned upon him savagely. ” Have you had a hand in this business In demanded. " Have you been plotting against me, like everyone else Lazarus Iles turned an imploring Flaw* pa Richard Bullock ; but Roach saw it. lie

' snapped his fingers, and taughed bitterly. " I knew you would, if it came to a pinch ; you're like all the rent," he suit' quickly. " Well, I'll be a match for tho whole lot of you yet. In the first place, Mr. Richard Bullock, I defy your authority, and I refuse to allow you to have anything to do with the girl who ia my ward. How do you like that ?" " I think we'd better settle first where the young lady said Richard Bullock stern- ly. " You say she has tied from this place —and with Mark Connaway P Where have they gone?" " I don't know—and I don't once," retort- ed Roach. "If you're no precious fond of the girl, look after her ; I've done with the jade. ' " That's very true," said Richand Bullock.

" But there is an account to be rendered of certain monies paid to you by her dead father. That father, in *dying, handed to me the papers drawn up in this house, and signed by you— I know Ihe exact amount of the fortune, and in what it was invested. I have theie papers with Inc now, and if you fail to give a proper account of your ,tewardship, MT. Roach, I most most reluc- tantly call in the Law to assist me." " Now, my dear Mr. Bullock," said Jaben Breec' h with a sudden change of manner— .. . .

" who should it he necessary" for us to lone our tempers over a little matter like this Of course you shall have all the information you require and I need not tell you that the dear girl', fortune is quite safe. Site's not been a 'void girl ; she's wilful and strong-willed, and perhaps I tnay have spoilt her a —"
"We won't go into that question, Mr. Roach," broke in the other. '' I have firot to find Madeline ; then we will go into the question of figures."

A "I shall be' only too pleased to be rid of the responsibility of Madeline's fortune,'" .id Mr. Roach, Inc brain busy already with plans for getting out of hic difficulties. "Come to me when you will, and everything shall he put before you." " Thank you, said the other shortly. " Now for another matter. When I came upon you in the stable to-night, there were three of you—you two, and another man who rushed pant me, and struck me, and seemed afraid of the very sight of me. That I believe was the man Neal Jarrow— was it not ?" •

"It was,- answered Roach. " Why was he afraid of me ; I have never met the man in my life." " It's not for me to nay," said Roach. "On that matter I have nothing more to tell you; you'd better sce Mr. Jarrow your.
-"-1 will—at the earliest opportunity," said Richard Buthick, buttoning his coat.

" Since you can give me no information about Madeline. I must do my beat to tind her myself, I suppose," he added. "And get your accounts ready, Mr. Roach; I may re- turn at any moment, and I shall Irani de- tails."

—lle's, at a sign from Roach, accompanied Richard Bullock to the door, and saw hltn stride away through the streets. In due course they were set down amid all the roar of the traffic of London, like two bad., lint in a wood, and oo left to shift for them- selves.

Madeline, is a way that NOIII4I have been delightful under other cir- cumstances, was determined to make the coot of this unconventional holiday; and she did not wish to have it curtailed. There was time enough to find her new guardian, Richard Bullock, she declared ; in London there were wonderful thiage to be seen, and wonderful things to be done. But we are troth penniless ; I can do nothing more for her. ' " And what about yourself ?" asked Rich- ard Bullock, looking at him intently. . .

div.head: ORIENT. CLOSE OF THE GREAT MISSIONARY EXHIBITION.
div.p: THE ORIENT. CLOSE OF THE GREAT MISSIONARY EXHIBITION.

The seven days exhibition held in the Parr Hall. which brought the "Orient " Tight to our very door., concluded last Thursday evening, after a successful week. Undoubtedly it Was the mon novel exhibition that has engaged the attention of the district, not only ham the point of view of the exhibits, but because of the wholehearted mingling together of Christians cf various denominations in a purely religious enterprise. The many thousands who attended were more than satisfied with the clear . insight they received into the manners and customs of the inhabitants of China, Africa, India, I West India, be. It must not be taken for granted that such ideas be con- ceived without the assistance of die lecturers, who gained portlier favour by their expositions. ,The opening ceremonies afforded the speakers the desir- able opportunity of appealing for more strenuous efforts on behalf of the Chriatianis,ng of those in foreign parts and we cannot but think that the result will te an awakened unsciousness in the minds of the people tf this district of the necessity of such a work.

THE EXHIBITION OPENED BY THE CHILDREN One of the molt pot. lee opening ca...nonies in con- nection with the Orient Exhibition wee tbet. of Satur- day, who, children from the various churches in the district provided quite an interesting feature. The audience was exceptionally large, and was presided over by 111neterliAlesander Ferguson, is to was evidently much at home in his new role. About TO children were dressed in their best, moat of the girls being da.niily attired in white. The chairmen was introduced by Eric Johnson and Kathleen Bawling after which Flora Watson clearly gave out the first hymn " From Green- lands icy mountains."Meater Ernest Hannan accompeny- ing on the piano. The CIIAIRNIAN said ha very much appreciated the privilege uf presiding over that re-opening ceremony. tie did not suppose that one boy in ten thousand ever got the chance of doing anything of the kind, and be was not likely to forget it as long nob, lived. (Hear, hear., He was not going to make one of the silly mistakes that slot of chairmen did and tnat wan to go on talking when everybody wished he would atop. (Laughter.) Although they were only boys and girls, they wanted to have their share in this great missionary enterprise. They hod beau looking forwsrd to thin exhibition for weeks, and now it tat cuma and the audience bad come, and the children had COMO; if they did not all do more, prey more and give more for foreign miesions then they had ever done before, be was afraid thecaen was hopeless. (Hear, hear and applause,. Greetings were conveyed by members of various churches, delightful short speeches being made by each. The repreaentatives incanted Mist Doris Wilkes (Church of EnglandhMiss Val Lockerbie (Presbyterian), , than Gyvendoliiie rhomas (Congregationalist Miss !Dorothy Bowdon (Baptist , Miss Marie Wild ; • Wesleyan), and Miss Mary Grillithe (Primitive Methodist), Th. choir then gave a superb rendering of "I bear ten thousand voices singing,' which WWI much appreciated •by the audience. Mies Non.% WlTlllota.ki. on rising to declare the ' exhibition open, Mb presented with a well arranged bouquet, by Miss Edith Richardson. She then spoke an follows (—Mr. Chairman, ladies end gentlemen,-1 am very pleased to be here this afternoon, to help Os the greatest work in the world, the trying to give all men • knowledge of God. The object of this exhibition is to interest the Church at home in Foreign Missions, to inspire all Christians with greater real in winning the world for Christ. This can only be accomplished by everyone of Us being in earnest about this part of Gods work, and sve cannot begin to work too young. I trust that this exhibition will be the means of deeply interesting a great number of children in Foreign Missions, sod 1 hove great pleasure in now declaring it !Ten, . . . .

He was sure that there was nobody who could look at the various exhibits without geating n very much clearer insight into the lives, manners and custome of those great races amongst which sootuch missionary effort was being carried or. If people would only understand a little mor• of what wee going on of what was being done f and what the difficulties were which the Christians had to cope with they would not have difficulty as they hail wow in arouniag enthusiasm for tns cause of the minions of Christianity. At the present moment there wan no part of the world which was causing 800,00 k anxiety, so much prayer, so much searching of heaftas the great East. Even allowing the average tonnage to be 10,000 and doubling the military allow. nice half, the ships of one line if one German Port could carry 50,000 men and stores, and at fifteen knots could cross from Hamburg to Yarmouth in 211 hours. The " unwieldly fleet " vi the first sea I rd, dissolves on examination. 3. Sir Arthur Wilson finally writes that if the inverters penetrated part of our Navy, their transom ts while landing their troops, will be sunk by our destroyers and submarines. This view 'eaves out of count that the opposing fleet also have a great flotilla of destroyers and subtuarines,and our three submarine bases on the East Coast are well known to them. As Colonel Repington points out, even if the invaders' transports are disturbed. their ships—or at least those which do not run into our many undefended ports—will anchor close inahme with only a few feet of water under their keel., so that even if submarine, can act in such shallow water and successfully torpedo the transports, these will only settle down upon the mud, and no great berm will be done. The fate of the transports sill be of little concern to us if the lar ding succeeds. The more closely tliese arguments are considered, the snore fully will the British people realise that . ships alone cannot save us. If we refuse either to pay or to play. we cannot in the ould etanil up against a rival, lavish both of service in her National Armv and financial effort for her growing Navy. Behind "a supreme Navy on the blue water, we must have a National Amy on the dry land—an army giving freedom to the Navy and strength of body and mind to the citizens.—Ymirs &c., • 13. S. TOWNROE.

div.p: AMERICAN DUMPING IN THE STEEL TRADE.

The " Economist " de% Gt., an inters-ding article to the American " dumping " campaign in the steel trade, t.l which there in some talk just now. The writer sacs that if our American rivals can pro- duce iron anti steel gnodi at a less cost than w eRn in this country. they have now a splendid opportunity of annexing the lion's share of the world's export trade in these product-, for the productive capacity of their works has been pushed far beyond their domestic demands. In 1909 the plants of the American Steel Corporation only worked up to 73 per cent, of their capacity. Last year the record was still worse. The aggregate productive capacity now standing RI!, is enormous. All that the Americans have todo in order to secure the trade is to quote below British and German prices , . . . .

But ran they do this? r The "Economist" is of opinion that they cannot. It p iuts out that " when I for • period of neatly a year and a half, following the financial disturbance of October. 1907, half the steel , mills in America were shut down. and DO great dumping " campeign was undertaken, we were told ' that the manufacturers, after working some years at . high pressure, welcomed the opportunity t f over- hauling their plants, relining their furnarea, scrapping old machinery and getting ready for the great boom of 191,..-10-11. Not only was old plant got in order for the good time coming, but new construction and extensipms were made. Productive rapacity Was enormously increased for the boom, but the boom Las not arrived an] is nowhere in sight." The writer then proceeds to show how greatly the 'CnSi ml reduction in the American steel trade has increased in recent years. " Ore, coal, coke and limestone are from 30 to Par per cent. dearer in America now than they were ipp the nineties. On top of ttpis, speculation 81111 frenzied tinstr.cial netliods have piled upon the American steel industry a colossal load of capital charges per ton of output. To-day the quotati, n is 'lt America did not heather competitors in the world's markets in the Mamie., she enema to stand little chance of doing so now. Spread over the last tell sears, the price of United States pig-iron has been re. per ton higher than the price of British iron. : Most e,r iron products have been correspondingly 'dear in the states. In the United States the coalfiehis . are so far removed from the iron ore supplies, the manufacturing plants are so far from both ate and coal. and are st such long distances from seaboard— which-means heavy CO•418 of assemblage and transit— and the burden of capital charges is so excessive, : that it is difficult to see how that country ran, in the ,1 long run, seriously challenge either Britain or Germany in the export trade in iron and steel.-
